title: Filling a prime grid that starts with the product eight
description: A three by three grid has row products eight, one hundred and five and seventy, and column products thirty, seventy and twenty eight. The video starts from the row of twos and fills the rest, and Keeko's doubt that two primes can swap places is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: start from the product with only one choice, then use the fact that each prime appears in a row only as many times as the row product allows. Watch for students who swap the pair in a column without checking the row.

source: Fill the 3 by 3 grid with prime numbers only so that the product of each row is the number to the right of the row and the product of each column is the number below the column. Row products: 8, 105, 70. Column products: 30, 70, 28.
video_script.why: The child fills the row that has only one choice, halves each column product, and then uses the primes each row allows to place the pairs.
video_script.substitution: Fill the row made of one prime, halve each column product, then place each pair using the row products.
video_script.anchor: an empty 3 by 3 grid with 8, 105 and 70 at the right of the rows and 30, 70 and 28 below the columns
video_script.wrong_answer: the three and the five can swap places
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the three and the five in the first column can swap places. Then the third row would hold a three, but seventy has no three, so the bubble is struck through.
video_script.payoff_line: The rows are two, two, two, then three, five, seven, then five, seven, two

final_answer.spoken: the rows are two, two, two, then three, five, seven, then five, seven, two

never_show: the three and the five can swap places
maths_rules: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2, so the top row is 2, 2, 2
each column has a 2 on top, so the two cells below make half the column product: 30 / 2 = 15 = 3 x 5, 70 / 2 = 35 = 5 x 7, 28 / 2 = 14 = 2 x 7
105 = 3 x 5 x 7 for the second row and 70 = 2 x 5 x 7 for the third row
70 has no 3, so the 3 of the first column is in the second row and the 5 is in the third row
the third row has one 5 already, so the second column puts 5 in the second row and 7 in the third row
the second row 3, 5 needs 7, so the last column puts 7 in the second row and 2 in the third row
video_script.design: One idea: fill the forced row first, then halve the column products and place each pair with the row products. Assumes the rules of the puzzle and prime factors. Wrong idea: the pair in a column can swap places. The grid stays on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is another puzzle from your book.
<bookmark mark='grid'/>Fill the three by three grid with prime numbers only.
<bookmark mark='right'/>The rows must multiply to eight, one hundred and five, and seventy.
<bookmark mark='below'/>The columns must multiply to thirty, seventy and twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What goes in the nine cells?

beats.on_screen: the grid holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a row of three boxes joined by times signs under the grid; the words each product is made of three primes

marks.rule: three boxes joined by times signs are drawn under the grid
marks.break: the words break each product into primes are written

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Each row and each column is three primes multiplied together.
<bookmark mark='break'/>Breaking a product into primes tells us which numbers it needs.

marks.given: the six products are written in two lines

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the six products around the empty grid.

beats.on_screen: To find: the nine primes in the grid

marks.find: the words the nine primes are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the nine primes that fit.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, 8 = 2 x 2 x 2, so the top row is 2, 2, 2; each column has a 2 on top, so the two cells below make half the product: 15 = 3 x 5, 35 = 5 x 7, 14 = 2 x 7

marks.top: the row that has 8 beside it is lit
marks.twos: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 is written and three twos drop into the top row
marks.half: 30 / 2 = 15 is written under the first column and 15 = 3 x 5 is written as a pair
marks.seventy: 70 / 2 = 35 = 5 x 7 is written under the second column
marks.last: 28 / 2 = 14 = 2 x 7 is written under the third column

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step one, start with the row that multiplies to eight.
<bookmark mark='twos'/>Eight is two times two times two, so the top row is all twos.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Every column now has a two on top, so the two cells below make half the column product.
Half of thirty is fifteen, which is three times five.
<bookmark mark='seventy'/>Half of seventy is thirty five, which is five times seven.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Half of twenty eight is fourteen, which is two times seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, second row 105 = 3 x 5 x 7, third row 70 = 2 x 5 x 7; 70 has no 3, so 3 goes in the second row and 5 in the third row

marks.rows: 105 = 3 x 5 x 7 is written beside the second row
marks.third: 70 = 2 x 5 x 7 is written beside the third row
marks.three: 3 goes in the first cell of the second row
marks.five: 5 goes in the first cell of the third row

narration: <bookmark mark='rows'/>Step two, the second row multiplies to one hundred and five, which is three times five times seven.
<bookmark mark='third'/>The third row multiplies to seventy, which is two times five times seven.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Seventy has no three, so the three from the first column goes in the second row.
<bookmark mark='five'/>That leaves the five in the third row.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, the third row has a 5, so the second column puts 5 in the second row and 7 in the third row; the second row needs a 7, so the last column puts 7 in the second row and 2 in the third row

marks.seven: 5 goes in the middle of the second row and 7 in the middle of the third row
marks.last: 7 goes in the last cell of the second row and 2 in the last cell of the third row

narration: <bookmark mark='second'/>Step three, the third row already has a five, and seventy has only one five.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>The second column holds a five and a seven, so the seven goes in the third row.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The second row has three and five, so it needs a seven in the last column. The two goes in the third row.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, check: 5 x 7 x 2 = 70; columns 2 x 3 x 5 = 30, 2 x 5 x 7 = 70, 2 x 7 x 2 = 28

marks.check: 5 x 7 x 2 = 70 is written beside the third row and a tick appears
marks.cols: 2 x 3 x 5 = 30, 2 x 5 x 7 = 70 and 2 x 7 x 2 = 28 are written under the columns with ticks

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check the third row. Five times seven times two is seventy.
<bookmark mark='cols'/>The columns are two times three times five, which is thirty. Two times five times seven is seventy, and two times seven times two is twenty eight.

marks.ans: the answer is boxed and the nine cells are filled
marks.all: all six products light up with ticks

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The rows are two, two, two, then three, five, seven, then five, seven, two.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Every cell is a prime, and all six products match.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the boxed answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt in a bubble beside the first column; 3 and 5 are swapped, the third row becomes 3, 7, 2 with 3 x 7 x 2 = 42 crossed out; the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: the bubble appears beside the first column
marks.swap: the 3 and the 5 in the first column trade places
marks.mult: 3 x 7 x 2 = 42 is written beside the third row with a cross

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the three and the five can swap places.
<bookmark mark='swap'/>Then the third row would hold a three, a seven and a two.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Three times seven times two is forty two, not seventy.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Seventy has no three, so the three must stay in the second row.
